articles.title: The future of commuter rail could be taking shape in Boston
articles.content:
This story was produced by Grist and co-published with StreetsblogMASS

Marvin Martin was in the Four Corners area of Dorchester one day when a train sped by on the Fairmount Line into downtown Boston. It was filled with white people, sitting comfortably and reading newspapers. It made him wonder why the commuter line seemed to pass through communities of color without stopping, leaving people in his neighborhood to crowd into buses.

Martin decided to do something about that. In 1995, he and others began pressuring the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority to expand service. It took more than 15 years, but the agency added three stops in Dorchester in 2012 and 2013. It opened a fourth in Mattapan in 2019.

But Martin wasn’t finished. He also had been pushing for electrifying the line.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“We want a train that would not be spewing a bunch of toxic particulates into the air,” Martin, who recently retired as the head of the transit advocacy organization Action For Equity, said.

Nearly three decades after Martin saw the train roll through Four Corners, the T, as the transit agency is known, plans to electrify the Fairmount line. It will lease seven battery-powered trains, each with four cars, for 15 years in a deal expected to cost $765 million. The arrangement allows the agency to gain experience with the technology before deciding whether to use it more widely.

The trains, built by the Swiss company Stadler, are slated for 2030. They will boost frequency of stops along the 10-mile route from every 30 minutes to every 20 and save 17,700 tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually compared to the diesels they will replace, according to the T.

Battery-powered trains allow transit agencies to electrify without the expense or complexity of installing overhead power lines, called catenary. But some worry the technology remains unproven on lines with ridership similar to what the Fairmount carries daily.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

They’ll find out soon enough. Caltrain, which provides regional service in the San Francisco Bay Area, plans to introduce battery-powered trains by 2028. Chicago’s Metra has a similar timeline. The projects could offer a glimpse into the future of rail electrification, but the technology must first show that it is capable of transporting thousands of people each day.

Boston is no stranger to electric rail. Its first electric streetcar rolled out in 1889, and the Tremont Street Subway — now part of the Green Line — was the first electric subway in North America. (It was third worldwide behind Budapest and London.)

Chris Friend, interim executive director of the advocacy organization TransitMatters, considers the Fairmount line a logical place to begin the T’s regional re-electrification because it is the system’s shortest commuter route. But he added that battery-powered trains have not yet been widely used on busy routes anywhere in the world. “So, is this the thing,” he asked, “or are we going to end up in another quagmire of an unproven technology?”

Battery-powered trains built by the French manufacturer Alstron are zipping back and forth on a 50-mile route in Germany that carries 2 million people annually. Dani Simons, the company’s vice president of communications in the Americas, said rising fuel prices make electrification more appealing. (The average price of diesel was $6.32 a gallon on Monday, up from $3.70 a year ago.)

Simons conceded the technology is best suited to “medium ridership.” But she said transit agencies should be pursuing electrification in all its forms, including diesel-electric hybrids and trains powered by overhead lines. These technologies can mitigate the impact of rising fuel costs and improve air quality. Even the MBTA is diversifying, with plans to deploy both battery and catenary trains on the Providence Line.

In some ways, electrifying transit means going back to the future. Urban systems began the transition from horse-drawn vehicles to electric streetcars in the 1880s and 1890s, said Albert Churella, a history professor at Kennesaw State University. Steam railroads, meanwhile, carried passengers between cities and their outskirts, helping spur the growth of suburbs.

Some commuter lines, including routes from New York to New Haven and Philadelphia to Paoli, along with the Long Island Rail Road, electrified at the start of the 20th century. Subways in Boston and elsewhere used electricity because steam trains emitted smoke and risked asphyxiating passengers underground.

It also helped that the technology was new.

“People get infatuated with technological advancements, and they tend to believe that these are cure-alls, that these are things that have extraordinary, almost unlimited potential,” Churella said. “Electrification of railways was no different.”

Most commuter lines, however, were never electrified. Many ran on tracks owned by larger railroads that also carried long-distance passengers and freight, operations that favored steam and, later, diesel power, said Nicholas Dagen Bloom, a historian and author of The Great American Transit Disaster. As passenger rail declined after World War II, he added, those companies increasingly wanted out of the passenger rail business. Diesel trains also offered a cheaper alternative to electrification because they do not need miles of wire.

Caltrain provides a look at what electrification can deliver. In 2024, it replaced diesel trains with electric ones on the 51-mile route between San Francisco and San Jose, powering them with overhead lines. Commute times dropped by as much as 23 percent because electric trains accelerate so much faster, and people loved the smoother, quieter cars. Ridership climbed 60 percent, and quality improved. Beyond the immense reduction in CO2 emissions, Joshua Apte, an environmental engineer at the University of California Berkeley, found that riders’ exposure to black carbon dropped 89 percent — a result he called comparable to what California cities achieved during 30 years of regulation.

Given the number of commuter rail systems that still rely on older diesel locomotives, “you might see similar air quality gains if you electrify them,” he said.

Although battery-powered trains might be slightly less efficient than those that use overhead lines or a third rail, Apte said they still do wonders for easing pollution.

That’s enough for Martin. He acknowledges that the cleaner, quieter trains that will begin rolling through the Four Corners will be a “novel thing” and that riders will continue breathing air polluted by diesel exhaust until they go in service. But he considers his three decades of advocacy a success.

“I’m pretty satisfied with where we ended up,” he said. “As long as we still get that train.”

articles.personality_title: Boston plans cleaner, battery-powered trains on Fairmount commuter rail
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For many years, people in Boston’s Dorchester neighborhood noticed that the Fairmount commuter rail line passed through their community without stopping, while mostly white passengers rode comfortably to downtown. Marvin Martin, a local resident, began pushing the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) to add stops and improve service for communities of color.

**What happened** – After years of effort, the MBTA added four new stops along the Fairmount line by 2019. Now, the agency plans to electrify this 10-mile route by 2030 using seven battery-powered trains. These trains will run more often, reducing wait times from 30 to 20 minutes, and cut 17,700 tons of carbon dioxide emissions every year compared to diesel trains.

**Impact** – This electrification is important because it will improve air quality and reduce pollution in neighborhoods that have long been underserved. Battery-powered trains don’t need expensive overhead wires, making the upgrade more affordable and faster to implement. Boston’s project will help test this newer technology, which could influence how other cities modernize their rail systems.

**What’s next step** – The MBTA will lease the battery trains and learn how well they work on busy commuter routes. Other cities like San Francisco and Chicago are also planning to introduce battery-powered trains soon. If successful, this could lead to wider use of cleaner trains across the country.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Boston’s move to battery-powered trains on the Fairmount line promises cleaner air and better service for neighborhoods long left behind by older diesel trains.

articles.title: Young people are bridging the climate divide for Oceania and the Caribbean
articles.summary: “The lack of strong and consistent climate policy means that every year, families lose loved ones, homes, and entire livelihoods because of climate-related disasters.”
articles.content:
By Adele Roeder, Orit Novak, Chelsea Adams and Zahiris P. Francisco

This article was originally published by Future Forward Australia on May 10, 2026. An edited version is published here with permission.

Young people are no strangers to seeing the impacts of climate change. In Australia alone, the catastrophic Black Summer bushfires of 2019–20, record-breaking floods across northern parts of the country in 2026, and most recently, the severe tropical cyclone Narelle, which badly affected three states, have all left their mark.

The livelihoods of Australian farmers are being severely undermined by prolonged droughts and a growing homeless population, more than 23 percent of whom are under the age of 25. Indigenous Australians, who have acted as environmental stewards for millennia, are seeing their knowledge, leadership, and deep cultural connection to the land undermined by practices like the desecration of sacred ceremonial sites by resource-extractive industries.

News headlines are often juxtaposed, highlighting these issues while simultaneously politicising a sustainable future through Australia’s reliance on coal, iron ore and natural gas. Even as the Great Barrier Reef bleaches, and Australian students skip school to strike for climate, the climate agenda is being quashed by political parties whose priorities are swayed by mining-magnate lobbyists.

Yet, young people living in Australia’s major cities have the privilege of being comparatively shielded from the worst impacts of climate change. In contrast, across Oceania and the Caribbean, Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are already experiencing the climate crisis as an everyday reality, despite contributing less than one percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.

What the climate crisis looks like across SIDS

While statistics help us understand the scale of the climate crisis across SIDS, they often fail to capture what this reality looks like. John Whippy, a community leader and climate activist based in Suva, Fiji, paints a different picture — one that moves beyond projections and into daily life. In coastal and low-lying communities, climate change is an immediate threat. Rising sea levels regularly push water into homes, forcing families to constantly adapt their living conditions. “When the water comes in,” he explains, “people have to move everything — put it higher, try to protect what they can.”

For many, relocation is not a viable option. Instead, communities are adapting in place. Homes are being rebuilt on higher foundations, using raised wooden structures in an attempt to stay above incoming water levels. These responses are practical and necessary, but they are also temporary and shaped by limited resources rather than long-term security.

Equally apparent is that the challenge is both environmental and social. Despite the presence of some external support — whether from governments, international organisations or limited local interventions — many communities are hesitant to seek assistance. Feelings of shame, exposure, or fear of becoming the subject of external attention can act as barriers to accessing help. As a result, communities often rely on their own means to cope.

‘Incomplete action’

Where external interventions do occur, they are not always sustained. Examples include development projects that began with intent but were never completed, infrastructure left unfinished, roads partially built, and drainage systems started and abandoned. In such cases, the issue is not simply ineffective aid, but the consequences of incomplete action. “If it’s not finished,” Whippy adds, “the water still comes. The problem just continues.”

These gaps highlight a broader issue within climate response efforts: a lack of continuity and accountability. With projects that are initiated but not fulfilled, responsibility is often left with the community, without the resources to complete what was started, raising critical questions about how climate solutions are designed, implemented, and evaluated.

From the perspective of those experiencing these impacts, there is a need for greater oversight — not just in funding, but in ensuring that initiatives are fully realised and genuinely beneficial — because there is a strong willingness within communities to engage. “If people come and talk to the community first,” Whippy notes, “everyone will help.” Collaboration, rather than imposition, emerges as a key principle. When communities are included in decision-making processes, when solutions are discussed, understood, and locally relevant, collaboration and participation follow.

Zahiris Priscila Francisco Martínez, a climate activist and journalist based in Santo Domingo, sees a similar situation unfolding across the Caribbean. “It’s heartbreaking to witness how every hurricane season becomes more severe,” she laments. “The lack of strong and consistent climate policy means that every year, families lose loved ones, homes, and entire livelihoods because of climate-related disasters. When heavy rains hit, children can’t go to school, adults can’t go to work, and the government is often forced to declare a national state of emergency.”

Read more: SIDS nations grapple with the climate crisis

The Dominican Republic, like many SIDS, remains highly vulnerable to climate extremes. Rising temperatures and warming ocean waters are intensifying storms across the Atlantic, increasing both rainfall and hurricane strength by the time they reach the Caribbean archipelago. Recent scientific analysis has shown that climate change is making hurricanes in the region more destructive, with stronger winds, heavier rainfall, and more rapid intensification.

For coastal and low-income communities in the Dominican Republic, these impacts are especially devastating. Flooding repeatedly affects families living near rivers, informal settlements, and vulnerable coastal zones, many of whom lack the resources to relocate or rebuild safely. Studies on Caribbean SIDS warn that rising sea levels, stronger tropical cyclones, and increasingly erratic rainfall patterns are placing enormous pressure on already fragile infrastructure, food systems, and public health networks.

‘When the water comes in, people can lose absolutely everything overnight’

“There is still so much more that could be done,” Francisco Martínez adds. “We need stronger prevention policies, resilient infrastructure, and more shelters for families living in high-risk areas. Here, just as in Fiji, when the water comes in, people can lose absolutely everything overnight.”

Francisco Martínez points to the growing number of tragedies linked to floods and infrastructure collapse across the region, where children and vulnerable families are frequently among the most affected. “For many people, even staying inside their homes during extreme weather becomes dangerous. It feels like being trapped between two impossible choices.”

Across the wider Caribbean, these challenges continue to intensify. According to UNICEF, the number of people internally displaced by storms and floods in Caribbean SIDS has increased sixfold in recent years, with children and young people among the most affected populations. Meanwhile, researchers confirm that over 65 percent of Caribbean SIDS populations live in low-elevation coastal zones, making entire communities increasingly exposed to sea-level rise, storm surges, disease outbreaks, food insecurity, and forced displacement.

“We have already seen tragic cases where children have lost their lives and infrastructure collapses have killed people in the streets,” Francisco Martínez says. “For families living in vulnerable areas, even staying inside their homes during extreme weather can become dangerous. It feels like being trapped between two impossible choices.”

Beyond physical destruction, climate change is also creating a growing emotional burden for Caribbean youth. Young people across the region are increasingly experiencing climate anxiety, fear, uncertainty, and ecological grief as they witness repeated disasters affecting their communities and futures. For many Caribbean youth activists, journalists, and community leaders, climate advocacy has therefore become not only an environmental issue, but a fight for survival, dignity, and justice.

Two sides of ‘voluntourism’

Responding to challenges of this scale requires more than short-term interventions or symbolic inclusion. The disconnect in the perception of the climate crisis is exemplified by the proliferation of “voluntourism,” where unskilled volunteers from high-income countries can seemingly “fix” climate issues in the Global South without community consultation, inherently promoting neocolonial notions.

Voluntourism involves combining travel with volunteer work which, while beneficial in certain contexts, frequently replaces place-based, community-informed and lasting change with feel-good, short-term input. Additionally, most programmes only involve short stays of up to three weeks — not nearly long enough to offset the emissions associated with participants’ travel.

With an estimated 10 million people partaking in voluntourism annually, it is clear that people want to help communities outside of their own. However, many voluntourism organisations continue to expand the climate divide by inhibiting sustainable development in the communities they work in through displacing local labour, excluding community input, and being culturally insensitive, not to mention exposing communities to additional issues like child safety risks and infrastructure strain.

Lasting solutions

This situation further emphasises the importance of prioritising locally informed and locally led solutions, and listening rather than assuming what kind of support vulnerable nations actually require from high-income countries.

Collaborative youth networks like the Oceania Caribbean Climate Alliance (OCCA) provide a more just and lasting solution. Such groups exemplify how young people from across regions, with different lived experiences of the climate crisis, can inform policy through local perspectives and push for equitable climate action.

A collaboration between the Global Shapers hubs of Brisbane and Castries, OCCA will host its Youth Climate Conference in Saint Lucia in December 2027, after rescheduling the event from 2026. The conference will fund young leaders from every Oceania and Caribbean nation for a two-and-a-half-day workshop on scaling climate projects from local to inter-regional, culminating in a Youth Climate Statement for decision-makers across both regions.

In July, OCCA also organised a North–South Ocean Dialogue in The Hague connecting young leaders from the Pacific and the Caribbean. These youth leaders are driving localised action with a global perspective, and supporting their cross-regional peers to effect change through shared resources, knowledge and community-building.

The Caribbean and Oceania are on the frontlines of climate change, but they are also home to the young people already shaping solutions with clarity and courage. For them, the task is not to step in briefly and step out unchanged, but to engage with care, humility, and long-term commitment.

If the goal is a fairer climate future, then how we show up matters just as much as what we do: impact means backing local leadership, not overshadowing it.

articles.personality_title_fr: Jeunes leaders d’Océanie et des Caraïbes unis pour lutter contre le changement climatique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les Petits États insulaires en développement (PEID) d’Océanie et des Caraïbes subissent de graves effets du changement climatique, comme la montée du niveau de la mer, des tempêtes plus fortes et des inondations. Ces impacts menacent les maisons, les moyens de subsistance et les communautés, en particulier les jeunes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des jeunes d’Océanie et des Caraïbes s’unissent via des groupes comme l’Alliance climatique Océanie-Caraïbes (OCCA). Cette alliance relie des leaders jeunes pour partager leurs connaissances et développer des projets climatiques adaptés à leurs besoins locaux. Ils prévoient une conférence jeunesse sur le climat à Sainte-Lucie en décembre 2027 pour promouvoir des politiques climatiques justes.

**Impact** – Contrairement aux actions bénévoles à court terme, ces initiatives menées par des jeunes se concentrent sur des solutions durables qui respectent les cultures et savoirs locaux. En travaillant ensemble entre régions, ils renforcent la voix des communautés et aident à créer des moyens concrets pour s’adapter aux menaces climatiques. Cette approche soutient les communautés vulnérables face aux défis quotidiens comme les inondations et les tempêtes.

**Prochaine étape** – L’OCCA poursuivra le renforcement des liens entre jeunes leaders et organisera des ateliers pour développer les projets climatiques. Leur prochaine conférence vise à produire une déclaration destinée aux gouvernements, encourageant des politiques qui favorisent un changement durable et le leadership local.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des jeunes d’Océanie et des Caraïbes mènent des actions collaboratives et locales pour faire face au changement climatique et protéger l’avenir de leurs communautés.
articles.personality_title_es: Jóvenes líderes de Oceanía y el Caribe se unen para enfrentar el cambio climático
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los Pequeños Estados Insulares en Desarrollo (PEID) de Oceanía y el Caribe enfrentan graves efectos del cambio climático, como el aumento del nivel del mar, tormentas más fuertes e inundaciones. Planean una Conferencia Juvenil sobre el Clima en Santa Lucía en diciembre de 2027 para impulsar políticas climáticas justas.

Al trabajar juntos entre regiones, fortalecen las voces comunitarias y ayudan a crear formas prácticas de adaptarse a las amenazas climáticas. Este enfoque apoya a comunidades vulnerables para manejar desafíos diarios como inundaciones y tormentas.

**Próximo paso** – OCCA continuará construyendo conexiones entre líderes jóvenes y organizará talleres para ampliar proyectos climáticos. Su próxima conferencia busca producir una declaración para los gobiernos, promoviendo políticas que apoyen cambios sostenibles y liderazgo local.

**Resumen en una frase** – Jóvenes de Oceanía y el Caribe lideran esfuerzos colaborativos y locales para enfrentar el cambio climático y proteger el futuro de sus comunidades.

articles.title: Carbon tracking tower put on Scotland's largest saltmarsh
articles.summary: It will track how much carbon is being taken out of the atmosphere by the saltmarsh on the Solway Firth.
articles.content:
New technology has been installed to track how much carbon is being taken out of the atmosphere by Scotland's largest saltmarsh.

The flux tower has been put in place at Caerlaverock on the Solway Firth.

About 85% of UK saltmarshes have been lost since the mid-19th Century as land has been reclaimed from the sea for agriculture, development or coastal flood defences, degraded through pollution or eroded by rising sea levels.

Corallie Hunt, coastal habitats adviser for NatureScot, said the installation of the first saltmarsh flux tower in Scotland marked an "important milestone".
articles.reasoning: The installation of a carbon tracking flux tower on Scotland's largest saltmarsh represents a significant environmental advancement by enabling precise measurement of carbon sequestration in a critical ecosystem. This helps inform climate action and conservation efforts on a meaningful scale, addressing the loss of saltmarshes and their role in carbon capture.
articles.personality_title: New tower measures carbon capture on Scotland’s largest saltmarsh
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Saltmarshes are coastal wetlands that help absorb carbon dioxide from the air. In the UK, about 85% of saltmarshes have disappeared since the mid-1800s because of farming, building, pollution, and rising sea levels.

**What happened** – A new device called a flux tower was set up at Caerlaverock on the Solway Firth, Scotland’s biggest saltmarsh. This tower will measure exactly how much carbon the saltmarsh takes out of the atmosphere.

**Impact** – This is the first time Scotland has installed a flux tower on a saltmarsh. It will give scientists detailed information on how well saltmarshes capture carbon, which is important for fighting climate change and protecting these valuable habitats.

**What’s next step** – The data from the tower will help experts understand how saltmarshes work and guide future efforts to protect and restore them. This could improve ways to use natural areas to reduce carbon in the air.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scotland’s new carbon-tracking tower on its largest saltmarsh will help measure and protect an important natural tool against climate change.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle tour mesure la capture du carbone sur la plus grande vasière d'Écosse
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les vasières sont des zones humides côtières qui aident à absorber le dioxyde de carbone de l'air. Au Royaume-Uni, environ 85 % des vasières ont disparu depuis le milieu des années 1800 à cause de l'agriculture, la construction, la pollution et la montée du niveau de la mer.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Un nouvel appareil appelé tour de flux a été installé à Caerlaverock, sur le Solway Firth, la plus grande vasière d'Écosse. Cette tour mesurera précisément la quantité de carbone que la vasière retire de l'atmosphère.

**Impact** – C'est la première fois qu'une tour de flux est installée sur une vasière en Écosse. Elle fournira aux scientifiques des informations détaillées sur la capacité des vasières à capturer le carbone, ce qui est important pour lutter contre le changement climatique et protéger ces habitats précieux.

**Prochaine étape** – Les données de la tour aideront les experts à mieux comprendre le fonctionnement des vasières et à guider les efforts futurs pour les protéger et les restaurer. Cela pourrait améliorer les méthodes pour utiliser les zones naturelles afin de réduire le carbone dans l'air.

**En résumé** – La nouvelle tour de suivi du carbone sur la plus grande vasière d'Écosse permettra de mesurer et protéger un outil naturel important contre le changement climatique.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva torre mide la captura de carbono en el mayor marisma de Escocia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los marismas son humedales costeros que ayudan a absorber dióxido de carbono del aire. En el Reino Unido, alrededor del 85 % de los marismas han desaparecido desde mediados del siglo XIX debido a la agricultura, construcción, contaminación y aumento del nivel del mar.

**Qué pasó** – Se instaló un nuevo dispositivo llamado torre de flujo en Caerlaverock, en el Solway Firth, el marisma más grande de Escocia. Esta torre medirá con precisión cuánto carbono absorbe el marisma de la atmósfera.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que Escocia instala una torre de flujo en un marisma. Esto dará a los científicos información detallada sobre la capacidad de los marismas para capturar carbono, algo importante para combatir el cambio climático y proteger estos hábitats valiosos.

**Próximo paso** – Los datos de la torre ayudarán a los expertos a entender mejor cómo funcionan los marismas y a guiar futuros esfuerzos para protegerlos y restaurarlos. Esto podría mejorar las formas de usar áreas naturales para reducir el carbono en el aire.

**Mensaje clave** – La nueva torre de seguimiento de carbono en el mayor marisma de Escocia ayudará a medir y proteger una herramienta natural importante contra el cambio climático.
